summary: I verified the clock and the causal chain as invariants across all 21 completed live runs and by reading trajectory.py, journal.py, envelope.py, resolution.py, llm.py, adapter.py and the kernel (world.py, simclock.py, events.py). Time monotonicity, the no-scheduling-past-cutoff rule, and the causal chain are genuinely sound: zero backwards-time records, zero events scheduled or committed beyond a cutoff, and every committed event in every ledger (including the 752-record case2_negotiation) resolves through event.fired -> event.scheduled to a real prior record with no dangling, forward or cyclic causes. Terminal citations are code-validated against the journal and every cited id exists. But the terminal-lineage rule fails where it matters most: 11 of 11 NO_AT_CUTOFF runs in the corpus reached that answer not by simulating to the horizon but because the event queue emptied days early, after which finish() jumps the clock across the untouched window in one record and licenses a final NO -- in four of them over 100% un-simulated time. The runtime has no deadline-driven scheduling at all (known_deadline is declared and wired to nothing, and the cutoff never enters any prompt), which is the direct cause. I also found the verifier's validator enforces no clock rule at all (a live NO_AT_CUTOFF four days early), MAX_EVENTS_PER_INSTANT measures the wrong instant (I reproduced 4 events on one instant), and the reserved final-judgment allowance provably cannot pay for the closing judgment.

findings.title: A final NO is licensed over time the trajectory never simulated: every NO in the corpus came from an empty queue, not from reaching the horizon
findings.evidence: sworldmodel/semantic_runtime/trajectory.py:823-834 breaks the loop on `ev is None or ev.t > cutoff` with no distinction between the two; line 948 then calls `finish("")` with truncated=False, so finish (757-791) advances the clock straight to the cutoff (769-777) and judges final=True, which is the only state in which NO_AT_CUTOFF is permitted. The sibling exits at 941 and 945 pass truncated=True precisely because 'the trajectory never reached the horizon, so nothing is known about what would have happened in the time that was not simulated' (docstring 757-768) -- but those two conditions never fire in production: budget_for(max_steps=250, actors=2, starting_events=1) = 18074 calls against a maximum of 393 observed, and max_steps=250 against a maximum of 114 steps observed. Measured over artifacts/simulations_v3/* and artifacts/matched_pairs/*: 11 of 11 NO_AT_CUTOFF runs stopped with an empty queue (scheduled - fired - cancelled = 0 before the cutoff), 0 of 11 ran out of steps or calls. Window actually simulated before the jump: b1_okafor_herrera__r3 0% (1 committed event, 1 step; ledger seq 26 at 2026-09-08T08:30 -> seq 27 `semantic.horizon_reached` at 2026-09-10T16:00, a 2d7h30m jump in one record, then seq 28 NO_AT_CUTOFF) -- and the world's own last judgment at seq 26 says the scanned lease 'is now on her computer, ready to be attached to an email'. case1_cold_email 0% (1 committed event, 1 step; ledger seq 21 at 2026-07-27T14:01 -> seq 22 horizon at 2026-08-10T14:00, the entire 14-day window jumped in one record, then NO_AT_CUTOFF). b1_okafor_herrera__r4 0%, b2_thornbury_lim 0%, b2_thornbury_lim__r2 1%, b1_okafor_herrera__r2 0%.
findings.why_it_matters: NO_AT_CUTOFF is a claim about the whole window -- 'the deadline arrived without the required events occurring' -- and it cites nothing, so the only thing justifying it is the absence of events across that window. In 11 of 11 cases most or all of that window was never simulated, so the justifying absence is not in the journal; it is an artifact of the scheduler having nothing left to pop. This is exactly the failure the design says it prevents ('that would turn a budget artifact into an answer'), and the protection is wired only to two conditions that provably never occur. An empty queue with days left on the clock is not evidence that nothing happens; it is evidence that nobody was asked.
findings.suggested_fix: Treat an empty queue before the cutoff as a truncation like any other -- pass truncated=True from the line 834 break unless the next queued event is beyond the cutoff -- so a run that stopped for want of anything scheduled reports `incomplete` and may not answer NO.

findings.title: Three of the five declared wake provenances are wired to nothing, and `known_deadline` in particular means the runtime can never schedule anything because a deadline is approaching
findings.evidence: sworldmodel/semantic_runtime/trajectory.py:154-158 declares WAKE_PROVENANCE = (actor_plan, observed_event, world_process, known_deadline, action_completion) and `_schedule_wake` rejects anything outside it (191-194). Only two are ever passed: `world_process` at line 369 and `actor_plan` at line 500; grep of the whole runtime finds no other `provenance=` argument. Across all 21 live runs, 222 wakes: {world_process: 140, actor_plan: 82}, and zero occurrences of observed_event, known_deadline or action_completion in any grounded_wakes.jsonl. `cutoff` is used in trajectory.py only as a scheduling bound (197, 350), a validator bound (689), the horizon advance (769) and the loop break (831) -- nothing anywhere schedules on account of it. It also never reaches a prompt: views.py:80-121 renders CURRENT TIME / WHO YOU ARE / evidence / observed / own actions / memories / what changed, with no deadline, and no `cutoff` appears in world_mind.py or actor_mind.py.
findings.why_it_matters: Scheduling is one of the things the governing rule says code owns, and the only mechanism by which an approaching deadline could put anything on the queue is declared and dead. That is the direct cause of the finding above: a run whose actors did not happen to volunteer a next_wake and whose world did not happen to volunteer a process has nothing left to do, days before the deadline everyone in the scenario is working towards, and the runtime simply stops. b1_okafor_herrera__r3 stops one step from the send with 2.5 days to go and 0 wakes outstanding; case1_cold_email stops after one turn with 14 days to go. A declared-but-unwired vocabulary member has already been the source of live defects in this codebase (see the comment at trajectory.py:650 about action_completion).
findings.suggested_fix: Wire `known_deadline`: when the queue would otherwise empty before the cutoff, schedule a known_deadline wake for each actor with an outstanding stake, or remove the three unused members so the vocabulary stops advertising scheduling the runtime does not do.

findings.title: The independent verifier's validator enforces no clock rule, so NO_AT_CUTOFF is accepted before the cutoff
findings.evidence: sworldmodel/semantic_runtime/resolution.py:212-251: `make_verifier_validator(known_event_ids, *, final=False)` takes no `now` and no `cutoff` and has no equivalent of the judge's check at 125-128 (`if status == "NO_AT_CUTOFF" and now < cutoff: raise`); its docstring at 213-215 states the omission is deliberate. The module docstring at line 14 nevertheless states the invariant as 'NO_AT_CUTOFF cannot be returned before the cutoff instant'. Live violation: artifacts/matched_pairs/a1_responsive__r2/ledger.jsonl seq 68, op `semantic.terminal_verification`, status NO_AT_CUTOFF, t = 2026-09-07T08:03:00+00:00 against a cutoff of 2026-09-11T17:00:00+01:00 -- four days early, and its own explanation reads 'the condition requires the reply to be sent before a deadline, but the deadline is in the future'. It contradicted the correct YES at seq 67 (citing e52, Marcus sending the reply), producing a disagreement that suppressed that YES; the same YES was re-proposed and agreed at seq 76/77 one step later. tests/test_semantic_runtime.py:1586, 1628, 1665, 1707 and 1854 have the fake verifier return NO_AT_CUTOFF unconditionally, so the gap is baked into the test fixtures rather than caught by them.
findings.why_it_matters: Half of the terminal machinery is operating on a premise the clock contradicts. It cannot directly manufacture a wrong NO, because agreement is required and the judge is gated -- but it can and did destroy a correct YES, and if the disagreement lands on the last scheduled event the run falls through to the horizon judgment and re-samples the answer over an un-simulated window (see the CRITICAL above). A code-owned time invariant that is enforced for one reader and not the other is not enforced.
findings.suggested_fix: Give `make_verifier_validator` the same `now`/`cutoff` parameters as `make_validator` and reject NO_AT_CUTOFF whenever `now < cutoff`.

findings.title: MAX_EVENTS_PER_INSTANT is measured on the instant the world was asked at, not the instant the event lands on
findings.evidence: sworldmodel/semantic_runtime/trajectory.py:246-251 computes `crowded` from journal events at `here = _iso_now(world)` plus queue entries at `e.t == world.clock.now` -- correctly including already-scheduled ones, as the comment claims -- but the floor at 343-346 is applied only when `delta.total_seconds()` is zero, and the destination `due = world.clock.now + delta` (349) is never crowd-checked. Reproduced deterministically with a scripted transport (no provider contacted): one actor turn emits MAX_INTENTIONS_PER_TURN=3 intentions at instant T, each drawing a world consequence of 'after: 1 hour', all three land at T+1h alongside the starting-event consequence -- 4 committed events on 2026-07-27T15:00:00+00:00 against MAX_EVENTS_PER_INSTANT = 3. The kernel's own same-instant backstop cannot catch this either: `World.schedule`'s MAX_SAME_INSTANT_DEPTH check (sworldmodel/world.py:140-145) only fires when `self._ctx_time is not None`, and `_ctx_time` is set exclusively by engine.py:138, which the semantic runtime never uses -- all 391 scheduled events across all 21 runs have depth 0.
findings.why_it_matters: MAX_EVENTS_PER_INSTANT is the only same-instant guard the semantic runtime actually has, and it protects only the instant the runtime is standing on. Several judgments made at one instant that all name the same delay converge on a common future instant with no cap at all -- the same 'one moment cut into pieces' the constant exists to stop, displaced by one hop. Live runs top out at exactly 3 so it has not yet bitten, but nothing in code prevents it.
findings.suggested_fix: Compute crowding against `due = world.clock.now + delta` after parsing the duration, and apply MIN_STEP_ON_A_CROWDED_INSTANT to the destination instant rather than only to zero-length steps.

findings.title: The held-back allowance cannot pay for the closing judgment, and the call ceiling is not a hard bound
findings.evidence: sworldmodel/semantic_runtime/llm.py:46 sets RESERVED_FINAL_CALLS = 2, documented as 'one call plus its one retry'. But the closing judgment is two calls, not one: trajectory.py:778 calls `judge(..., reserved=True)`, which for any non-UNRESOLVED status calls `_verify` at 717 -- so up to 2*(MAX_RETRIES_PER_CALL+1) = 4 attempts must fit in a reserve of 2. Reproduced with a scripted transport at max_calls=5: a single retry in the closing judge yields `traj.status == "failed"`, `traj.answer is None`, on a run with a complete record (the CallBudgetExceeded from `_verify` re-enters finish at trajectory.py:955-962 and the second judge call is also unaffordable). Retries of the judge role do occur live (runtime_metrics.json: judge retries=1 in case1_cold_email and case2_negotiation). Two further leaks: trajectory.py:747 passes `reserved=True` on EVERY `_verify`, including the mid-run ones invoked from the in-loop judge at 934, so ordinary verification spends the reserve; and llm.py:145-150 checks the ceiling once before the retry loop and appends an entry per attempt, so a call that starts one below the ceiling ends one above it -- the same probe recorded 6 provider calls against max_calls=5.
findings.why_it_matters: The reserve exists for exactly one situation -- the budget is spent and the run still needs an honest closing judgment -- and in that situation it provably does not work: instead of `incomplete` with an answer, the run reports `failed` with no answer at all, losing a complete trajectory. Reachability is low in practice because budget_for is enormous relative to observed usage (18074 vs <=393), which is also why this has never been exercised. The ceiling overrun separately means max_calls is not the hard bound the docstring claims.
findings.suggested_fix: Set RESERVED_FINAL_CALLS to 2*(MAX_RETRIES_PER_CALL+1), stop passing reserved=True on mid-run `_verify` calls, and re-check the ceiling inside `ask`'s retry loop.

findings.title: The ledger's terminal lineage records proposed terminals but never records whether one was accepted
findings.evidence: sworldmodel/semantic_runtime/trajectory.py:703-708 writes the OP_TERMINAL record with the first judge's status BEFORE `_verify` runs at 717, and the disagreement branch at 726-732 appends nothing to say the answer was refused. artifacts/matched_pairs/a1_responsive__r2/ledger.jsonl seq 67 is therefore a `semantic.terminal_check` with status YES that the run did not accept, followed by seq 68 disagreeing, with no record of the refusal. replay.py:150-153 reports `terminal_status` as the last OP_TERMINAL record's status regardless of whether it was agreed, and evaluation/summarise_runs.py:41 and evaluation/matched_pair_result.py:43 read `answer.status` without consulting `trajectory.status`.
findings.why_it_matters: The ledger is supposed to be the authoritative record. A reader of the ledger alone -- including the replay verifier -- cannot tell whether a terminal was claimed or refused, so a run that ended in `disagreement` would be reproduced and tabulated as having reached the status its first judge proposed. No run in the current corpus ends in disagreement, so this is latent rather than observed.
findings.suggested_fix: Append a record of the adjudicated outcome (agreed / disagreement) after `_verify`, and have replay report that record rather than the last OP_TERMINAL.
